answer.summary: When forced to choose, Anuj Rathi prefers excellence: think carefully and ship better, because many experiments can be recognized as likely failures before they waste company time. It is a preference, not an absolute rule; the choice depends on risk and market context.

sections.heading: His preference and reasoning
sections.content: Rathi says to “think more and ship better” when forced to choose. He believes smart teams can use metathinking to identify experiments that are obviously likely to fail and avoid trying them, saving company time. He calls this a preference rather than a rule, and says speed and excellence are separate axes—ideally, a team improves at both, but if it must choose, choose excellence.

sections.heading: When speed may still make sense
sections.content: His interview framework considers risk and how well the team understands the market and competition. Rathi contrasts a poorly differentiated, nonviable product with a case where there is a clear competitive distinction and market gap; in the latter, he says launching a half-baked version to get user feedback can be acceptable.
